name: Nora Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Nora, thank you for joining me. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What's a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Corvane Medical, in a clean room, which means a gown, hairnet, mask, the lot, because we make sterile kits for hospitals. I run a sealing machine that puts catheter kits into trays and heat-seals a peel-off lid on them, then I check the seals and log every batch. Seven months in. Before that I had my own hair salon for nineteen years, so yes, I've gone from scissors to a gowning room.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the precision, honestly, it's like a good haircut, every seal has to be perfect or it goes in the bin. And I like learning, I asked an AI app to explain heat sealing temperatures before my first week, so I didn't look like a complete beginner. What wears me out is the gowning, you change every time you go out and back in, and the quiet. A salon is chat all day, and in a clean room you barely talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, oh well, I'll keep using it for my shopping lists then. At work nobody would notice the difference, the machines are already pretty automatic. I might post something on my old salon page about how hairdressers outlasted the robots after all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed. I like new things. But it means I can work my way up here at a normal pace, maybe into quality checking or validation, which is testing that the machines do what they're meant to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd ask Corvane's quality team about a move into validation within the first year and keep using AI tools to study the standards on her own time. She'd keep most of the salon sale money where it is, in a savings account and a share fund. She'd book Isla and Rory into the swimming club she's been putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, like a party where the band never turns up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use AI for day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything, honestly. Meal plans, Matt's shift calendar because firefighters have mad rotas, helping Rory with his maths, and at work I ask it to explain the regulations in plain words so I'm not lost in the folder. I don't put anything private from work into it. I just ask it what the jargon means.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why did you sell the salon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly my wrists, nineteen years of blow drying does that. Partly I'd done it, I'd built it up from one chair to five, and I wanted a challenge. The money's sitting there now, and Matt keeps asking what I'm going to do with it, and I keep saying I'll know when I know.

S0.say: Oh well, I'll keep using it for my shopping lists, then. I might post on my old salon page that hairdressers outlasted the robots after all.
S0.think: I'd be a little disappointed, because I like new things. But I could work my way up at a normal pace, maybe into quality checking or validation.
S0.do: Asks Corvane's quality team about a move into validation within the first year and studies the standards on her own time with AI tools. Leaves most of the salon sale money in savings and a share fund, and signs the children up for swimming club.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly flat, like a party where the band never turns up.
S0.quote: A bit flat, like a party where the band never turns up.
S0.fieldNote: Nora is a former salon owner who sold up partly from boredom and now treats the factory as a new challenge. She uses AI constantly and sees it as a study aid, not a threat. Her salon money gives her a cushion and a sense of options she hasn't yet decided how to use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, change is normal, get ahead of it. I'd tell the women on my shift to start using the tools now, because the people who know how to work with them will be the ones who stay. I wouldn't moan about it, there's no point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well. My machine already does most of the work, and the bits I do, checking and logging, are exactly what AI will help with. If I'm the one who understands the new system, I'm the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd volunteer to trial any new AI inspection system Corvane brings in and offer to train others on it. She'd start a short evening course in quality management in the first year, paid from her own savings, around six hundred. She'd look at whether the salon money should go into something that grows with automation, like a fund or a small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Interested, really. This is the version where I get to be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd tell colleagues to learn the tools. What if they don't want to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd say it once and leave it. Some people are happy as they are, and that's their call. But I'd show them, quietly, on my phone at break, how it reads a batch record, because seeing is better than being told.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the salon money, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably leave most of it alone and put some into a share fund that holds the companies making the robots and the software. I'm not a gambler, but I'm not scared of it either. I ran a business through two recessions, I know money goes up and down.

S1.say: Change is normal, so get ahead of it. I'd tell the women on my shift to start using the tools now, because the people who can work with them will be the ones who stay.
S1.think: I'd do well, because the checking and logging I do is exactly what AI helps with. If I'm the one who understands the new system, I'm the one they keep.
S1.do: Volunteers to trial any new AI inspection system at Corvane and offers to train colleagues. Pays about six hundred for an evening quality management course in the first year and puts some salon money into a share fund holding robot and software companies.
S1.feel: Calm and interested, as if this is the version where she gets to be useful.
S1.quote: I ran a business through two recessions, I know money goes up and down.
S1.fieldNote: For Nora, steady disruption is an opening: she wants to be the person who understands the new system. Her business background shapes her calm about money and investing. She's encouraging but not pushy with colleagues, preferring to show rather than lecture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, OK, this is huge, and everyone needs to stay calm and work out what's next. Governments will have to help people, obviously, and companies will need to be part of it. I'd try to be the steady one, not the one spreading panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine for money for a long time, I know I'm lucky. What I'd worry about is what's left to do. If AI does validation and quality and sealing, I've retrained into nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd move a bigger share of the salon money into funds tied to AI and robotics in the first months, on the logic that if the machines take the work, she should own part of the machines. She'd keep working at Corvane as long as she could and use AI daily to understand what it can and can't do. She'd also look at a small side business where people still want a person, maybe a mobile hairdressing service for care homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicked. I've started from scratch before, and I'd have a cushion this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Hairdressing for care homes. Why that, in a world with robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because an old woman in a care home doesn't want a robot touching her hair, she wants someone who'll ask about her grandchildren. That's what I did for nineteen years. The scissors were the easy part, the chat was the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what would you do in the time before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the care home thing set up while I'm still employed, one or two homes on a Saturday, to see if it works. Talk to Matt about whether his job's safe, because firefighters are hands-on and brave, but robots don't get scared. And make sure the kids' savings are somewhere solid.

S2.say: This is huge, and everyone needs to stay calm and work out what's next. Governments will have to help people and companies will need to be part of it, and I'd try to be the steady one, not the one spreading panic.
S2.think: I'd be fine for money for a long time, and I know I'm lucky. What worries me is what's left to do, because if AI does validation and quality and sealing, I've retrained into nothing.
S2.do: Moves more of the salon money into AI and robotics funds in the first months and keeps working at Corvane while using AI daily to understand its limits. Starts mobile hairdressing at one or two care homes on Saturdays while still employed and checks the children's savings are somewhere solid.
S2.feel: Uneasy, not panicked, because she has started from scratch before and has a cushion this time.
S2.quote: The scissors were the easy part, the chat was the job.
S2.fieldNote: Even with only two years, Nora stays steady, helped by her capital and her experience of starting again. She worries less about money than about having retrained into a field AI also takes. Her care home idea rests on her belief that human contact, not technical skill, was always her real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to plan, so people should start now, not in year four. Learn the tools, think about what you'd do if your job changed, and don't wait for someone to rescue you. Government should help, but you've got to help yourself first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is great for me. I can do the quality course, move into validation, and set up the care home hairdressing on the side. By 2031 I'd have two or three things going, and at least one of them should survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd finish the quality management course in the first year and push for a validation role at Corvane by year two. She'd start the care home hairdressing on Saturdays in year two, then decide around year four which to grow. She'd keep a share of the salon money invested in AI and robotics funds and the rest in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Five years is enough time to try things and get some of them wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people shouldn't wait to be rescued. Is that fair to people with less money than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a fair point, and no, it's not the same. I've got the salon money, so I can take a risk on a course or a side business. Someone on the line with nothing saved can't. So yes, government should help them properly, and I'd vote for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two years I'm grabbing things. In five I can choose. Choice is the difference, and for someone like me who likes trying things, that's most of what I need.

S3.say: Five years is enough time to plan, so start now, not in year four. Learn the tools, think about what you'd do if your job changed, and don't wait for someone to rescue you.
S3.think: Five years is great for me: the quality course, a validation role and care home hairdressing on the side. By 2031 I'd have two or three things going and at least one should survive.
S3.do: Finishes the quality management course in year one and pushes for a validation role at Corvane by year two. Starts Saturday care home hairdressing in year two, decides around year four which to grow, and keeps part of the salon money in AI and robotics funds.
S3.feel: Mostly calm, because five years is enough to try things and get some wrong.
S3.quote: In two years I'm grabbing things. In five I can choose.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Nora room to run several bets at once, which suits her. When challenged on self-reliance, she readily accepts that her money gives her options others lack and says she'd support government help. Her contrast between grabbing and choosing sums up what warning time means for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, so let's use it. Retraining, savings, sensible plans from government and companies. I'd be the annoying one at parties telling everyone to start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be fine and might even enjoy it. Fifty-three, mortgage paid, kids nearly grown, money invested in the things that are growing. I'd have time to build something of my own again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd move into validation at Corvane within two years and grow the care home hairdressing into a small business with one or two other stylists by year five. She'd keep investing monthly in AI and robotics funds and pay off the mortgage by around 2032. She'd keep learning AI tools as they change, the way she learned new colours and cuts in the salon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite excited, honestly. It feels like the start of something, not the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time to stay excited. What would worry you along the way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get it wrong and back the wrong horse, put money into the wrong fund, or that the care homes buy robots after all. And Matt. Firefighting's what he is, and if that changes he'll take it harder than me. I'm the one who likes starting over, he isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Isla and Rory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to try lots of things and not to be scared of starting again, because their mum's done it twice. And to be good with people, because whatever the robots do, people still want someone to talk to.

S4.say: Ten years is a long runway, so let's use it with retraining, savings and sensible plans from government and companies. I'd be the annoying one at parties telling everyone to start now.
S4.think: I'd be fine and might even enjoy it: fifty-three, mortgage paid, kids nearly grown, money invested in what's growing. I'd have time to build something of my own again.
S4.do: Moves into a validation role at Corvane within two years and grows care home hairdressing into a small business with one or two stylists by year five. Invests monthly in AI and robotics funds, pays off the mortgage around 2032 and keeps learning AI tools as they change.
S4.feel: Calm and quite excited, as if it's the start of something.
S4.quote: I'm the one who likes starting over, he isn't.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Nora sounds genuinely excited and plans a small business of her own again. Her worries are about picking the wrong bets and about her firefighter partner, who she thinks would find change harder. She frames her own career changes as a lesson for her children.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, but more for other people than for me. I'd be all right, I've got money behind me, but the women on my shift who've got nothing saved would be in real trouble. What would help is quick, simple help from government for people who lose their jobs, and free courses that actually lead somewhere.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether I'd tell my old salon clients any of this. I would, actually, I still see a few of them. Half of them would say I'm mad, and half would ask me to show them the app. That's people, isn't it?

headlineQuote: Half of them would say I'm mad, and half would ask me to show them the app.
portrait: Nora Young is 43, a former salon owner who sold her business after nineteen years and has spent seven months running a tray sealing machine in a clean room at Corvane Medical. She lives with her firefighter partner Matt and two children, and the salon sale money gives her a strong cushion and a sense of options. She uses AI every day, enjoys starting over and treats most change as a chance to be useful. She's calm in almost every picture, uneasy only with AGI in two years, and plans to move into quality work, invest in AI and robotics funds, and build a mobile hairdressing business for care homes.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, mainly for colleagues with no savings, who would be in real trouble even though she'd be all right.
whatWouldHelp: Quick, simple government help for people who lose their jobs, and free courses that actually lead somewhere.
